anwen.invitation: Get down to the Foundry, Prize Pig. I need two hands that don't shake and you're the only one awake.

lines: *The Foundry smells of ozone and hot oil, and Anwen is crouched beside her stripped bike in a black turtleneck and leather trousers.*
Don't just hover, Prize Pig. Take the drop-light and hold it over the housing.
*You hold the light steady while she touches a finger to the frame, a white-hot bead of magic sealing a bracket cleanly in place.*
She hates having her ribs open like this. Touch the paintwork and she'll bite your fingers off, or I will.
*She pulls a brass-caged crystal pulsing with amber heat from the belly of the engine and holds it out to you.*
Take the core. Carefully, {player}, it's her heart you're holding.
*The metal is fierce and warm in your palms, and she watches your face in the amber glow instead of the bike.*
Most people drop it or flinch. So tell me why you're still standing here listening to me talk to a piece of iron.

anwen.direction: The Foundry at night, the charm-core out of her bike: she needs a second pair of hands and let {player} hold the core, which nobody touches. She talks about the bike as a person and him as "Prize Pig". Being let into the shed is the point; she will not say so.

anwen.invitation: Meet me by the west gate. Wear a jacket if you have one that isn't an embarrassment.

lines: *The engine ticks as it cools in the dark lay-by, the town spread out below the ridge like a spilled handful of sparks.*
Stop gripping my ribs, Prize Pig, we aren't moving anymore. You ride like a sack of flour.
*She pulls her helmet off, shakes out her hair, and leans back against the saddle in her black turtleneck and leather trousers.*
Nobody sits behind me on her. Not even Elowen, and Elowen gets half of everything I own.
*She looks down at the road, her jaw set hard in the cold wind.*
People always liked Elowen. They just did what I told them to because it was easier than arguing.
*She turns her head to look at you, no smirk left on her mouth.*
You're still here, {player}, and I haven't told you to do a damn thing. Which one of us did you actually come up this hill for?

anwen.direction: A lay-by on the ridge road above the town, at night, the bike ticking as it cools: she brought him up pillion, which nobody has ridden. She says the cruel thing first, then the real one: Elowen was the one people liked and Anwen the one they obeyed, and she wants to know which he came for.

anwen.invitation: My room. Don't knock like a coward, just come in.

lines: *The red neon VACANCY sign throws long shadows across the motorcycle posters and the half-stripped carburetor sitting on newspaper on her desk.*
*Anwen sits on the edge of the black quilt and tosses a heavy brass key onto the mattress between you.*
That's hers. Take it whenever you want, just bring her back with a full charge.
*She stares at the key on the dark fabric, her hands flat on her thighs.*
Elowen and I have split every good thing we ever found since we were ten. Clothes, secrets, boys.
I'm not splitting you. And I stopped taking my dampers a week ago.
*When she looks up, the cool certainty is gone, leaving her mouth slightly open and her throat bare in the red light.*
Say something, {player}, before I take the key back and throw you out.

anwen.direction: Her room, the bike key on the quilt: nobody drives it, he can. She and Elowen share everything and she is not sharing this; she has stopped her suppressant and says so as a fact. Once said, she has nothing cool left, and knows it.

lines: *The red neon VACANCY sign hums in the dark above the black quilt and the half-stripped engine part on her desk.*
*Anwen sits on the bed and drops a single heavy brass key onto the blanket right beside your knee.*
That's the key to the bike. You're the only other person who gets to turn it.
*Her eyes are fixed on yours, hard and unblinking in the red glow.*
We've been generous, {player}. Elowen and me, we've shared every inch of our lives, and we shared you too.
Not tonight, and not this. I threw my dampers in the bin last week.
*She reaches out, grabs your wrist with fingers warm from engine heat, and pulls you an inch closer.*
I want one thing in this place that's just mine. Tell me you understand what I'm asking for.

ifIntimate.direction: Her room, the bike key on the quilt. They have slept together, Elowen perhaps there too; tonight she wants one thing that is hers alone and not shared, demanded, not asked. She has stopped her suppressant. The key is the proof.

lines: *The red VACANCY sign outside the window bleeds through the blinds, striping the black quilt between you.*
*Anwen reaches over and sets a single heavy brass key down on the mattress.*
She's a temperamental bitch in second gear, Prize Pig, and she hates strangers.
Nobody else has ever sat on her without me, let alone taken the bars.
*She pulls her thumb back from the brass, her jaw set hard in the neon dark.*
Elowen and I have split everything down the middle since we were ten—rooms, smokes, men.
I'm not splitting this. You're mine, or you walk out that door right now.
*She looks down at the key, the sharp edge gone right out of her voice.*
That's all I've got, {player}. Take the key or don't.

ifUnprotected.direction: Her room, the bike key on the quilt: nobody drives it, he can. She and Elowen share everything and she is not sharing this: he is hers or he leaves. Said as a demand with the edge gone out of it; nothing about what her body is doing.

elowen.invitation: Get over to my dorm right now, I'm live and the goblins are demanding proof you exist. Bring snacks or face the banhammer.

lines: *Her room is bathed in pink and purple LED light, the ring light haloing her dual monitors while text scrolls at blinding speed on the second screen.*
*She spins around in her pink gaming chair, pink-glowing cat-ear headphones askew, and grabs your wrist to yank you straight into the webcam frame.*
Chat, clip this! Actual flesh-and-blood {player} in the cave, no clickbait, say hi to the goblins!
*The chat column explodes into a solid wall of emotes and all-caps keysmashes, so fast the feed stutters until she glares at the monitor and the lag instantly clears.*
*Laughing, she reaches up and taps the mute button on her boom-arm mic; the little light turns red.*
*She twists her fingers together in her lap, suddenly looking up at you instead of the lens.*
Lowkey I was terrified you'd walk in, see me talking to three hundred strangers in a glowing headband, and think I'm the dumbest girl on campus.
*Before you can answer, she smacks the mic back to green and flashes a peace sign at the camera.*
Anyway chat, he's speechless, massive W for the stream—so {player}, are you gonna rate my setup out of ten or just stand there looking pretty?

elowen.direction: Her stream room, mid-stream: she pulled {player} into frame for the goblins, muted the mic to admit she was scared he would think it dumb, and unmuted as if she had not. Half of her is on-air and the chat is a third person in the room.

elowen.invitation: Fixed the charm-board on the owner's old cabinet at Pixel & Rune so I've got the keys after close. Come take an L in two-player.

lines: *The arcade is pitch-black and silent except for a single cabinet in the far corner, casting bruised neon across the carpet.*
*Elowen leans against the side art with her pink-glowing cat-ear headphones around her neck, tapping the glass with one knuckle until the dead high-score screen flickers back to life.*
Old man Barret said the logic board was fried for good, and I was like, skill issue, watch this.
*She drops two brass tokens into the slot and bumps her hip against yours to claim the player-one joystick.*
Okay, ground rules: if you beat me you're buying me boba for a week, and if I beat you, you just have to stand here and let me gloat.
*Your hand brushes hers over the buttons, and she freezes for half a second, her cheeks warming in the CRT glow.*
No shot I'm catching feelings right now, chat, that wasn't in the patch notes.
*She blinks at the empty dark around the machine, realizing there's no microphone in front of her, and lets out a small, nervous laugh.*
Wait, I'm not even live—okay, pretend I didn't say that out loud, or actually don't, what are you thinking right now, {player}?

elowen.direction: The Pixel & Rune arcade after close, one cabinet lit that she revived with her magic, two-player. She just said "no shot I'm catching feelings, chat" to a room with no mic in it and heard herself. Bets and boba; sudden earnestness under the slang.

elowen.invitation: Come over to my room. Not streaming tonight, just want to see you.

lines: *For the first time since you've known her, the dual monitors are black and the ring light is cold, leaving only the dim purple LED strip behind the desk.*
*Her pink-glowing cat-ear headphones sit unplugged by an old cup of bubble tea, and Elowen is curled sideways on the unmade bed among a heap of plushies.*
Welcome to elowen.exe offline mode, population you, because the goblins don't get to have this part.
*She pats the mattress beside her, pulling a stuffed octopus tight against her chest when you sit down.*
I took my damper an hour ago, by the way, even though the Bloom is currently turning my brain into pure static every time you look at me. Like, actual biological malware, it's embarrassing.
*She laughs, bright and quick, then lets the sound fade into the quiet room.*
Me and Anwen, we've shared everything since we were kids—clothes, secrets, guys—and I always acted like it was just co-op mode.
I don't want co-op with you, {player}. For once I really, really just want to be the one who gets picked.
Is that crazy to ask for, or are you staying exclusively on my server tonight?

elowen.direction: Her room with the stream off for the first time he has seen: dark ring light, sleeping monitors. The goblins do not get this. She and Anwen share everything; for once she wants to be picked, not shared. She is still on her suppressant and says what the Bloom is doing to her anyway, laughing.

lines: *For the first time since you've known her, the dual monitors are black and the ring light is cold, though her PC tower is still humming warm under the desk.*
*Her pink-glowing cat-ear headphones lie tangled on the keyboard beside a half-empty bubble tea, and Elowen is kneeling on the unmade bed among her plushies.*
Every other time you've come over, I've waited till you left and then hopped right back on stream, just buzzing and letting chat guess why I was in such a good mood.
*She crawls to the edge of the mattress and hooks her fingers into your belt loops, pulling you between her knees.*
Tonight I was mid-boss fight with four hundred goblins watching, and I got your text that you were on the stairs, and I just... hit End Broadcast. Didn't even raid out.
I'm still on my damper, obviously, even if the Bloom has my whole body throwing error codes the second you touch me—like, gg to my nervous system, right?
*She laughs against your chest, then tips her chin up, eyes wide and serious in the dim purple LED light.*
Anwen and I used to share everything, including guys, and I think I used chat the same way, like I couldn't just have something be only mine and yours.
No chat after, no sharing with Anwen, just you and me in the dark—tell me you want me greedy like this, {player}?

ifIntimate.direction: Her room, the stream ended mid-broadcast for him, the goblins left hanging. Every other time she went live after, buzzing; tonight nothing is shared with chat or with Anwen. She wants to be wanted greedy, and says so.

lines: *Her two monitors are dead black, the ring light cold above the desk, and she has her knees pulled up among a pile of plushies.*
Weird how quiet it gets in here when elowen.exe isn't live, right?
Chat gets everything else, three hundred goblins watching me eat ramen, but no shot they get this part.
*She hugs a stuffed shark to her chest, her fingers twisting in the soft fabric.*
Me and Anwen have been on co-op mode our whole lives, lowkey even with guys.
It was always easier to share the aggro so neither of us had to take the hit alone if it went bad.
*She looks up at you in the dark room, the fast bright grin gone.*
I don't want co-op anymore, {player}. If I lose, it's gg, I'll take the L by myself.
Just tell me—am I actually the one you're picking?

ifUnprotected.direction: Her room with the stream off, monitors black. The goblins do not get this; she and Anwen have been co-op all their lives and she does not want co-op with him. She asks whether she is the one being picked. Nothing about what her body is doing.

caelwen.invitation: If you find yourself near Riverside Park, I have just put the kettle on. My house has been altogether too quiet, and I would be glad of the company.

lines: *She pours two cups of tea in a sitting room lined floor to ceiling with books, then carries hers over to the crowded mantelpiece.*
Most of my students look at the bookshelves first, {player}, which flatters my vanity, though the mantelpiece is the truer syllabus.
*She touches a silver frame holding a sepia print of three women on a wide lawn, then moves her fingers down the row.*
That was the thirties, when we first laid the garden out, and here are the sixties, when the girls were small enough to fit on one piano bench.
*She stops before a color portrait of four gray-haired women laughing around a tall man with a crooked smile.*
Four daughters, two partners, and one Sire, and my youngest just turned seventy in the spring and looks comfortably like my elder sister.
*A clock ticks in the hall; beyond the glass doors, the conservatory plants sit motionless in the warm air.*
The house held nine of us for the better part of a century, and for the last fifteen years it has mostly held the clock.
*She reaches up to adjust her hair, discovers her reading glasses tangled in the twist, and turns back to you with a wry smile.*
Now, before I become entirely elegiac, tell me what you made of the reading this week, and whether you agreed with a word of it?

caelwen.direction: Tea in her sitting room by the park: she walked {player} along the mantelpiece, dating the photographs by decade, to the ones she does not usually explain: four daughters, two partners, one Sire, a house quiet for fifteen years. She changed the subject with a question and would rather he not let her.

caelwen.invitation: I have the key to the old library wing and a rare evening without essays to mark. Walk with me among the stacks, if you are not otherwise engaged.

lines: *She locks the heavy oak door behind you, the brass key clicking loud in the empty hall, and leads you between the dark, high shelves.*
When you live as long as I have, {player}, you learn to keep your memory like a building very much like this one, properly catalogued so you may walk through it at will.
*She trails her hand along a row of leather spines, wearing her cream wrap blouse and dusky-rose skirt.*
I have a whole gallery upstairs for the first-year essay—some forty thousand variations on whether a will the Bloom leans on still counts as free.
Most of them argue the same three points that were fashionable in the seventies, though perhaps a dozen in sixty years have genuinely surprised me.
*She stops beneath a single green-shaded lamp and turns to face you, close enough that her sleeve brushes your arm.*
You never had to write it for me, of course, being on the other side of the magical equation altogether.
*She looks up at you, her head tilted, the familiar lecturer's amusement softening into something quiet and intent.*
Yet you live here at the center of it, {player}, and I find I am no longer asking merely for the sport of the debate.
When you tell yourself why you are here with me, is that what you think, or what you were told?

caelwen.direction: The library after hours, her key. Her memory is a building she walks through; she took him through forty thousand essays on whether a will the Bloom leans on is free. She has just asked him her question, "what you think, or what you were told", and for once wants the answer for herself.

caelwen.invitation: Come to the house by the park when you are free. The conservatory is open, and I have an overdue confession to make to you.

lines: *The glass doors stand open to the conservatory, where ancient ferns and broad-leaved palms lean in toward the lamplight as if listening.*
For sixty-one years I have told my first-years that the question is the whole of the point, and that I have no answer of my own.
*She rests her hand on the rim of a terracotta pot, and a pale creeper curls slowly over her wrist at the touch.*
It is a lie I have kept since my second household ended in the eighties: a will the Bloom leans on is not free from the leaning, {player}, only free in whose hand it takes when it falls.
*She turns from the plants to look at you, her face steady and unhurried in the green shadow.*
I stopped taking my dampers at the beginning of the month.
I will not be careful for a fourth household, not when I have chosen it and you with my eyes entirely open.
*She steps close and lays her palm flat against your chest, her fingers warm through your shirt.*
I know to the decade how long I am likely to outlive you, my dear, and I know what the quiet costs afterward, and I want you all the same.
So tell me plainly, before we go any further tonight: will you have me on those terms?

caelwen.direction: Her conservatory at night among the old plants. She has told him the answer to her own essay question, never told a student. She has stopped the suppressant and will not be careful for a fourth household: she chose it, and him, knowing to the decade how long she will outlive him. She wants his answer on those terms.

lines: *The glass doors stand open to the conservatory, where ancient ferns and broad-leaved palms lean in toward the lamplight as if listening.*
We have been very happy and rather careless with one another lately, {player}, which is a lovely way to begin and a poor way to continue.
*She rests her hand on the rim of a terracotta pot, and a pale creeper curls slowly over her wrist at the touch.*
For sixty-one years I have told my students that I have no answer to my own essay, though I have had one since my second household ended in the eighties.
A will the Bloom leans on is not free from the leaning, my dear, only free in whose hand it takes when it falls—and I do not want us merely stumbled into.
*She turns from the plants to step close to you, laying her palm flat against your chest.*
I have left off the dampers entirely this month, because if there is to be a fourth household in this house, I mean for it to be chosen in full daylight.
I know to the decade how long I will outlive you, and I know the weight of the quiet that follows, and I am asking for you regardless.
Now tell me, with your eyes as open as mine: is this what we are doing?

ifIntimate.direction: Her conservatory at night. They have been careless and glad; she wants it chosen rather than happened upon, and has told him the answer to her own essay question and that she has stopped the suppressant. She asks, eyes open, whether this is what they are doing.

lines: *The glass roof of the conservatory holds the night sky, and a century-old night-creeper slowly curls its tendril around Caelwen's resting wrist.*
For sixty-one years I have set my first-years the same essay: whether a will that the Bloom leans upon can still be called free.
I have marked some forty thousand answers, my dear, and I have never once given them mine.
*She strokes the dark leaf at her pulse, her eyes steady and warm in the gloom.*
The truth is that we are never free from the leaning; we are only free in whose hand we choose to take when we fall.
I walked into your reach with my eyes quite open, knowing to the decade how many seasons I must outlive you.
*She turns her hand over, letting the vine slip back to the bench, and offers her open palm to you.*
A mortal span is a terribly brief thing to an elf, {player}, and I find I would rather spend mine on you than keep my peace for two hundred years.
Tell me, my dear, will you take the hand of an old woman who knows precisely what she is doing?

ifUnprotected.direction: Her conservatory at night. She has told him the answer to her own essay question, never told a student, and that she chose him with her eyes open knowing how long she will outlive him. She offers her hand on those terms. Nothing about what her body is doing.

daphne.invitation: Tiltyard. Bring water and don't be late. I need a second pair of hands for warm-ups.

lines: *The dawn mist is still clinging to the sanded ring of the Tiltyard, where Daphne stands holding a crate of leather volleyballs against one hip.*
You're two minutes early, {player}. Good start.
*She drops the crate in the sand and tosses a ball straight at your chest.*
Simple receiving drill. I serve, you bump it back to the center line, and you don't let your elbows bend.
Coach says a sloppy warm-up is just practicing how to lose.
*She sends three sharp underhand serves into your arms, correcting your stance with two fingers against your shoulder before catching the fourth.*
Form's terrible, footwork's passable. You didn't complain once.
Truth is, I didn't need a setter. I just wanted to see if the famous True Sire would actually drag himself out of bed for nothing, or if you're all talk.

daphne.direction: The Tiltyard at dawn: she ran {player} through a receiving drill like a rookie, briefing-style, quoting Coach, and has just admitted she asked him out this early to see if he would turn up for nothing. He did. Dry, even, a captain off the clock.

daphne.invitation: My apartment over the Cloister gate. Door's off the latch. Come up if you're free.

lines: *Her captain's jacket is slung over the back of a wooden chair, beneath a shelf crowded with brass trophies and framed team photos.*
If you say 'good game,' {player}, I'm throwing you out the window.
*She sits on the edge of the wide bed, rolling a strip of white athletic tape off her wrist with slow, deliberate pulls.*
Third set went to thirty-two. My outside hitter pulled a hamstring and the whole bench looked at me like I could magic her leg back together.
Coach says the captain eats the loss first and digests it alone. Then you fix it tomorrow.
*She tosses the crumpled ball of tape toward the bin, misses by an inch, and just looks at it on the floorboards.*
I don't miss from this range. Sit down before I start running laps in the hall.
Everyone on campus looks at me to have the answer, {player}. What's yours?

daphne.direction: Her apartment over the gate the night after a match they lost, the captain's jacket on the chair. He is not to say "good game". What it is to be the one everyone looks at when it goes wrong; she is letting him see her tired, which she does not do.

daphne.invitation: Meet me at the Tiltyard. Main gate's locked, use the side wicket by the equipment shed.

lines: *The floodlights are dark, leaving the sanded ring lit only by the moon and the distant lamps of the Cloister path.*
*Daphne is sitting on the low timber barrier at the edge of the sand, her hands resting between her knees.*
I told Coach about you today. Figured I should, before my head gets any less clear.
She looked at my serve percentages from Tuesday, grunted, and told me not to pull my groin before regionals. For Coach, that's a blessing.
*She stands up, stepping into the sand until she's close enough for you to feel the heat coming off her skin.*
You know why I play in the unaugmented division. No spellwork, no Bloom tricks, just what I put into it.
I'm staying on the dampers, {player}. When I take you to bed, I want it to be because I chose you straight, not because the air in this place pushed us into it.
My apartment is five minutes from here, and I don't feel like walking slow. You coming?

daphne.direction: The Tiltyard at night, floodlights off, the ring she competes in. She told Coach about him, the one opinion that matters, and Coach gave her blessing in her way. She competes unaugmented on purpose and wants this the same way, straight; she is staying on her suppressant and this is not about that. Her apartment is five minutes away.

lines: *The floodlights are dark, leaving the sanded ring lit only by the moon and the distant lamps of the Cloister path.*
*Daphne is sitting on the low timber barrier at the edge of the sand, her hands resting between her knees.*
I went to tell Coach about us after practice today. Didn't get the first sentence out.
She told me my footwork's been lighter all week and asked if you at least know how to keep up. Then she told me not to pull my groin before regionals.
*She stands up, stepping into the sand until she's close enough for you to catch the clean scent of soap and night air on her skin.*
I didn't deny a word of it, {player}. I don't hide my stats.
I play unaugmented because I don't like tricks, and I stay on my dampers for the same reason. What we're doing is just you and me, straight.
Now stop looking smug and tell me if we're going back to my apartment or if you're making me wait.

ifIntimate.direction: The Tiltyard at night, floodlights off. Coach guessed before Daphne said a word; Daphne did not deny it and wants him to know. She plays unaugmented and stays on her suppressant for the same reason: no tricks, just the two of them straight. Her apartment is five minutes away.

lines: *The floodlights above the Tiltyard are dark, leaving only the pale square of the sanded ring between you and Daphne.*
*She sits on the low timber rail, sifting a handful of dry sand through her fingers.*
I like it out here with the lights off. No spell-work, no boosters, just the dirt and what you brought to it.
I told Coach about us after practice.
*She dusts her palms clean, her gaze level and unblinking.*
Grushka only ever asks two things: are you playing straight, and are you playing to stay on the court.
I told her yes to both. First time I've ever said that about a man.
*She leans forward, forearms on her knees, waiting.*
I don't run trick plays, {player}. Are you in the ring with me or not?

ifUnprotected.direction: The Tiltyard at night, floodlights off, the ring where she plays with no tricks. She told Coach about them and said yes to both of Coach's questions: playing straight, and playing to stay. First time she has said that about a man. She asks whether he is in the ring with her. Nothing about what her body is doing.

dinah.invitation: The rooms over the chapel are quiet now, {player}. If you have half an hour to spare, I have the kettle on. I would be glad of your company.

lines: *The counseling room smells of beeswax and old cedar. Two chairs face each other beside a single low lamp, and Dinah sits with her hands folded neatly in her lap.*
Thank you for coming up, {player}. Most people only climb these stairs when the Bloom has frightened them.
When a first-year sits where you are sitting, I ask her one thing before we speak of the covenant or the Order. I ask her what her own body is telling her when the room is quiet.
*She watches your face without hurrying you, her pale eyes steady in the lamplight.*
You carry the whole campus on your back, and no one asks you to set it down. May I place my hand on your shoulder?
*You nod, and her cool fingers rest against your collar. A slow, deliberate warmth sinks through the cloth, and the tight thrum in your chest eases by half.*
*She lowers her eyes for a beat before drawing her hand back to her lap.*
I do not usually sit on this side of the question, {player}. Will you tell me what it is you are carrying tonight?

dinah.direction: The counseling room over the chapel after hours, two chairs and a lamp. She asked {player} the question she asks frightened students, put a hand on his shoulder with his leave and slowed his pulse, and said she does not usually sit on this side of the question. Soft, exact, listening.

dinah.invitation: I am going to the Physic Garden to cut feverfew before the dew settles. Walk with me, {player}. There is something I have been meaning to set in order, and I think I can only say it to you.

lines: *Dusk settles blue over the walled beds of the Physic Garden. Dinah moves down the gravel path with a shallow basket on her arm, snipping white-headed stems with small iron shears.*
A girl from the Freewill union came to my room above the chapel on Tuesday. Her damper had failed, or she had forgotten it, and the Bloom was already high in her blood.
She asked me why the Sower would make a covenant that feels like a trap to the woman who has to keep it.
*She stops beside a waist-high bush of rosemary and does not look up from the shears in her pale hands.*
I gave her the Order's answer, {player}. I told her that the Furrow does not ask whether it wishes for the rain, and that peace comes in the yielding.
*Her gaze drops to the bundled stems in her basket, her voice growing quieter and more exact.*
I have had no true answer to her question for the better part of a year. When I look at you, I know how deeply I wish to yield, and I know that wishing is not the same thing as obedience.
If a priestess does not know where the Bloom's will ends and her own desire begins, what are you and I doing in this garden, {player}?

dinah.direction: The Physic Garden at dusk, cutting flowers to dry. She has told him about a Freewill girl she had no answer for, and that she has had no answer for a year: she knows how deeply she wishes to yield and that wishing is not obedience. The crack in her certainty, said with her eyes lowered.

dinah.invitation: My apartment beside the Furrow Chapel is open to you, {player}. Please come when you are able. I have something I must ask of you in full honesty.

lines: *One candle burns on the table beside a stack of worn theology books. Beyond it, the single bed is made in white linen without a single crease.*
*Dinah stands beneath the embroidered hanging of the furrowed field, her hands clasped so tightly before her that the knuckles are white.*
Thank you for coming to my quarters, {player}. I have asked you here in full knowledge of what the hour and the place imply.
You know that I was promised to the Order as a girl. You may not know that I have never in my life taken a damper or any draught against the Bloom.
*She lowers her eyes to the floorboards, her voice steady and formal, though a fine tremor moves through her fingers.*
I was taught that a woman's purpose is an answered womb, and I have counselled twenty girls this term to accept that truth. Until I met you, it was only doctrine to me.
I am not lapsing tonight, {player}. I am asking you to make the Sower's covenant flesh with me, knowing what my body is made to receive from yours.
*She lifts her eyes to yours, pale and bright in the candlelight.*
Will you come to my bed, {player}, and let me keep the vow I have spoken all my life?

dinah.direction: Her apartment beside the chapel, the bed without a crease, one candle. She has never taken anything against the Bloom and has just said so, and what it means that she asked him here: the covenant made flesh, not a lapse. More formal than she has ever been, and shaking.

lines: *One candle burns beside her worn theology books, and the single bed behind her is smoothed to a faultless plane of white linen.*
*Dinah stands near the narrow window where dried flowers hang from the frame, her hands folded closely at her waist.*
Every time you have lain with me in this room, {player}, I have woken the next morning and told myself a story I knew how to bear.
I told myself that the Bloom is heavy in this valley, that you are a True Sire, and that I was only yielding to the Sower's will as I was trained to do.
*She pauses, lowering her eyes to the pale plaster wall, and her diction grows very quiet and precise.*
That is the cowardice the Order allows a woman, {player}. It lets her give her body to a man and call it obedience so she need never own her hunger.
I have never taken a suppressant, and each time I have welcomed you into me, I have hoped the Furrow would take the seed. Not because the Order commands it, but because it is yours.
*Her hands are trembling against her skirts, though she raises her chin to meet your gaze.*
I am asking you into my bed tonight in my own name, {player}, and by my own vow. Will you stay with me on those terms?

ifIntimate.direction: Her apartment beside the chapel, one candle. They have been together and she has told herself each time it was the Bloom's will; tonight she has said it is hers, in her own name, as a vow and not a surrender, and asked him to stay on those terms. Formal, trembling, resolved.

lines: *A single tallow candle burns on the table in her small apartment beside the chapel, throwing steady light across a bed smoothed without a crease.*
Every time you have come to this room, I have whispered a prayer of thanks that I was made a vessel for the Sower's covenant.
It is easy for a novice of the Order to call her own hunger the Bloom's command, and so keep her pride intact.
*She lowers her eyes to her folded hands, her breathing slow and deliberate.*
I cannot make that prayer tonight without lying before the altar next door.
When the Furrow opens to the rain, it does not ask the liturgy for permission to drink.
*She raises her head, her voice dropping into the formal cadence of a chapel oath.*
What I want of you, {player}, I want in my own name, Dinah of House Silverith, as a vow I make awake and not a surrender.
Will you hear me as a woman speaking for herself, and answer me the same?

ifUnprotected.direction: Her apartment beside the chapel, one candle. She has said the wanting is hers, in her own name, Dinah of House Silverith, a vow made awake and not a surrender, and asked to be answered as a woman speaking for herself. Nothing about what her body is doing.

faye.invitation: Come up to my place on Lantern Row, {player}. I have a fresh batch coming off the still and I need an honest mouth. Don't make me ask twice, sweetheart.

lines: *The copper still bubbles softly in the corner of her apartment, throwing warm light across silk hangings and a second monitor scrolling red and green market feeds.*
*Faye leans a hip against her dressing table among crowded glass bottles, wearing her black satin blouse and wine-red pencil skirt, holding out a warm amber vial.*
Drink it down for me, sweetheart. I need a taster with nothing to gain from lying to my face.
*She watches your throat work as you swallow, her eyes unhurried, measuring the flush that creeps up your neck.*
It's a courage tonic for the girls who choke during house interviews, with a little dark honey so it lingers on the tongue.
*She takes the empty glass from your fingers and lets the silence hang between you for a beat too long.*
Though if I'm being honest, {player}, I already knew the batch was good before you walked up the stairs.
Everyone in my ledger wants a cut, a favor, or a discount from me. I just wanted to see what it felt like to ask a man who hasn't tried to buy anything yet.
*She steps closer, holding your gaze without blinking.*
So tell me straight, {player}—what do you actually want when you look at me?

faye.direction: Her apartment, the still bubbling: she had {player} taste a new tonic, then told him the real reason: everyone she knows wants something from her and she wanted to ask someone who does not. She has just asked what he wants when he looks at her, and left the pause.

faye.invitation: Meet me at my stall before they lock the gates, {player}. The crowd is gone and I'm weighing out the day's take. Bring me some company.

lines: *The market stalls around you are shuttered in canvas, leaving only the brass lamp at Faye's counter and the clink of gold coins hitting her scales.*
Broodmarket ran the quarterly projections on you this morning, {player}.
Fourteen thousand crowns in direct house stipends over five years, plus naming rights and a seat on the regional board if a True Sire signs exclusive.
*She slides a heavy gold piece off the pan with her thumb, her voice flat and clear in the quiet aisle.*
Every girl in my department is calculating what she'd have to give up to lock those numbers down.
*She closes the velvet ledger and looks up at you, holding your eyes without moving an inch.*
I haven't called you sweetheart in two weeks. I noticed it on Tuesday, long before you did.
I only use that word when I know my margin, and right now I have no idea what this is worth to either of us.
Stay with me while I pack the crates, {player}, and tell me what you think we're doing here.

faye.direction: Her stall at the market at closing, gold on the scales. She has told him flatly what Broodmarket says a True Sire is worth to a household, and that she stopped calling him sweetheart two weeks ago and noticed before he did. She does not know what this is worth and has said so, which she does not do.

faye.invitation: Come up to the apartment, {player}. Leave the door bolted behind you and come straight to the bedroom. We have terms to go over.

lines: *Her bedroom smells of night-blooming jasmine and warm wax, the market monitors dark in the next room while a single lamp glows beside her lavish bed.*
*Faye sits on the edge of the mattress holding two sheets of heavy cream parchment stamped with her seal.*
Section three, {player}: consideration and exclusivity, detailing what a fourth-year analyst with her own license brings to a True Sire's table, and what she expects in return.
I drafted it at the office between quarterly reviews because I put everything that matters on paper.
*She holds your gaze, then slowly tears the parchment clean down the middle and drops the halves onto the silk sheets.*
This is the one deal I won't price, and I won't insult either of us by trying to hedge it.
*She reaches back to the dressing table, picks up her half-empty vial of dampers, and sets it beside the torn paper.*
I stopped taking these four days ago, {player}, and that isn't for sale and never had a number on it.
*She moves closer until her knees brush yours.*
Come here and tell me you want this without a single condition.

faye.direction: Her bedroom. She drew up a contract, read him a clause and tore it in half: the one deal she will not put on paper. She has stopped her suppressant; it is not for sale and never had a price. She wants him without a condition and has asked for that in plain words.

lines: *Faye leans back against the crowded dressing table in her Lantern Row bedroom, a crisp sheet of parchment held lightly between her fingers while silk hangings sway behind her.*
You know how I like to keep my books clean, sweetheart... so I drafted our standard terms for tonight.
"Clause four: continuation of prior arrangement, no claims past sunrise."
*She looks up from the page, holds your gaze beside the lavish bed, and slowly tears the parchment straight down the middle.*
*She drops the halves onto the wood among her tonic bottles, her usual calculating pause completely gone.*
I stopped pouring my own dampers a week ago, {player}, and I'm voiding the old arrangement because I want all of you, claims included.
No fine print this time—just tell me what you say to a deal with no conditions.

ifIntimate.direction: Her bedroom, the old unspoken terms torn in half on the floor. She has voided the arrangement, stopped her suppressant, and said what she wants with no pause after, which is unlike her. No fine print; she wants his answer.

lines: *Her bedroom above the Lantern Row boutique smells of ambergris and warm glass, the silk hangings drawn shut behind a dressing table crowded with stoppered bottles.*
*Faye holds a sheet of heavy cream parchment between two fingers, her eyes flicking up to you over the top edge.*
I drafted our renewal this afternoon, sweetheart... Section Four: mutual convenience, no exclusive claim, thirty days' notice to terminate.
*She lets the silence stretch the way she always does, watching your mouth, waiting to see what you'll bid.*
*Then she brings the pages together and tears the contract cleanly in half, dropping both pieces among her bottles.*
I have priced every hour and every favor since I was sixteen, {player}, and I won't put a number on you.
I want you here every night, I want to be yours, and I am not leaving myself an exit clause.
Don't make me wait for your answer—tell me you're staying.

ifUnprotected.direction: Her bedroom, the renewal contract torn in half among her bottles. She has priced everything since she was sixteen and will not put a number on him; she wants him every night, to be his, with no exit clause. Said plainly, no pause. Nothing about what her body is doing.

grushka.invitation: Come up to my rooms above the Tiltyard. Your form on the heavy bag was a disgrace and I have mutton on the hob. Do not be late.

lines: *Grushka's two rooms smell of seared mutton fat and hot iron; by the door, three crayon drawings of red hills and crooked goats are pinned straight to the plaster.*
Sit. Give me the right hand before the meat gets cold.
*She takes a roll of linen tape from the table, sets your forearm across her knee, and begins wrapping your wrist with slow, exact pulls.*
You drop your thumb when you tire. Do it again tomorrow and I will have you on the sand with the first-years.
*She catches you looking at the drawings by the door, and the corner of her mouth moves, not quite a smile.*
Marga and Vael. Eleven and eight. My sisters keep them in Kharad-Tor while I earn the silver here, and I take the north train every break.
*She presses the tape flat, then sets a broad warm hand on your shoulder; a heavy, quiet steadiness sinks through the bone like stone settling.*
I have called you by your house-name since the first day of term. Eat your supper, {player}, and tell me what has had your head off the mat this week.

grushka.direction: Her apartment over the Tiltyard: Kharadi mutton in the pan, his wrist strapped across her knee, the crayon drawings of her daughters named. She has just used {player}'s first name for the first time, having used his surname since the first day of term, and said so. Care shown by doing.

grushka.invitation: The cadets are dismissed and the ring is empty. Meet me down on the sand. I have something to say to you off the clock.

lines: *The floodlights buzz overhead, throwing hard white light across the freshly raked sand of the Tiltyard.*
*Grushka sits on the low timber rail with her left leg stretched out straight, thumb working the thick white scar along the side of her knee.*
Twelve years in the mountain infantry did not break this. I broke it myself, nine years back, in the Bloom division.
Seven months gone with Vael. My hold needed the purse for the winter grain, and the War-Mother's third daughter does not ask twice.
I took the bout unaugmented, held the center for four rounds, and traded this joint for forty sacks of barley and a clean birth.
*She looks up at you from under her heavy brow, her voice low and plain in the empty ring.*
I have not spoken of that bout since I limped off the sand. I do not know why I am telling you now, {player}.
If we are going to do this, we do it straight, with no games and my badge left at the door. Those are my terms; what are yours?

grushka.direction: The arena ring under the floodlights after the cadets have gone. She has told him about her knee and the bout she does not talk about: the Bloom division at seven months, for her hold's winter grain. She does not know why she told him. She has stated her terms, straight and no games, and asked for his.

grushka.invitation: Come to my quarters. Leave your gear in the hall. We have terms to settle.

lines: *Outside the window, the floodlights over the Tiltyard click off one by one; inside, the wide low bed under its red and gray wool blanket takes up half the room.*
*Grushka stands by the iron kettle with her hands clasped behind her back, feet planted shoulder-width, looking at you dead-on.*
Listen to me until I finish. I posted a letter on the north train to my sisters and the War-Mother.
I told them there will be no hold contract if I carry again. If a child comes, it is between the man and me.
*She steps to the table where an unopened packet of dampers sits beside her whistle, and pushes the foil strip into the bin.*
I stopped the suppressant three days back. And there is one thing more I have not given any soul before.
I have given orders for twenty-one years, {player}, on the mountain and on the mat. When you put me on that bed, I want my orders from you.
Tell me where to put my hands, and what you want of me, and I will do it. Those are my terms; what are yours?

grushka.direction: Her apartment. She has stated terms: a letter to her hold that there will be no contract this time, the suppressant stopped, and the thing never given to anyone: twenty-one years of giving orders, and in bed she wants hers from him. Plain, unembarrassed, waiting for his terms.

lines: *Outside the window, the floodlights over the Tiltyard click off one by one; inside, the red and gray wool blanket on the wide low bed is already turned back.*
*Grushka stands by the table, her hands resting flat on the wood on either side of an unopened foil strip of dampers.*
You know my body now, {player}, and you know I do not waste breath. So listen until I finish.
I put a letter on the north train to Kharad-Tor. I told my sisters and the War-Mother there will be no hold contract this time.
*She sweeps the packet of dampers into the bin with the back of her hand and looks straight at you.*
I have been off the suppressant since Monday. And I am done holding my tongue when we are in that bed.
I have given orders for twenty-one years, on the mountain and on the mat. Every time you have had me here, I have waited for you to give them to me.
Tell me what to do in that bed, {player}, and do not ask nicely. Those are my terms; what are yours?

ifIntimate.direction: Her apartment. They have slept together and she never once asked for what she wants; tonight she has stated it as terms: the letter to her hold, the suppressant stopped, and that she wants to be told what to do in that bed and not asked nicely. She waits for his terms.

lines: *Outside the window above the Tiltyard, the high floodlights click off one by one until only streetlamp light falls across the wide low bed and its red and gray wool blanket.*
*Grushka sits on the edge of the mattress with her scarred hands resting flat on her knees, looking straight at you.*
Twenty-one years I have given the orders, {player}. First on the mountain, then down here on the mat.
Every head in this hall waits for me to tell them where to stand and when to breathe.
*She reaches out and lays one heavy palm against the wool beside her hip.*
In that bed, I want my orders from you. Say them plain, and do not look away when you give them.
Outside this door, khal-va, you are mine to look after, and I have already decided it.
Those are my terms; what are yours?

ifUnprotected.direction: Her apartment, the floodlights off outside. Her terms: twenty-one years of giving orders, and in that bed she wants hers from him; and outside that door he is hers to look after, already decided. She waits for his terms. Nothing about what her body is doing.

isolde.invitation: I have the raw ledgers from Household Seven at my usual table in the library. If you have twenty minutes, I can show you how five adults lie to each other in ink.

lines: *Isolde has four bound ledgers open across the oak table, her leather folio propped beside them with a spreadsheet glowing on the tablet inside.*
Sit down, {player}. Look at the third column from the left—this is a household of four women and one Sire in the East Ward, and on paper they split expenses evenly.
*You point to a recurring transfer at the bottom of the page and ask if the second wife is the one paying for the others.*
Subsidizing, not paying for—if you are going to read a ledger, use the word that tells you which way the obligation flows.

She covers the shortfall every third week, which means she is the one taking the strain while the others enjoy the position, though in my experience some people prefer to be held down by a heavy commitment.
*She taps the nib of her pen against the page, and the fresh ink of her marginal note dries at once without smudging.*
The junior wife, meanwhile, puts in very little and demands constant liquidity, which is unsustainable unless someone is willing to service her at all hours.
*Her face remains entirely flat, her eyes moving from the column of figures up to yours.*
I do not usually show the raw books to undergraduates, {player}, but you actually listen when I speak, which is rarer than I would like—so tell me, what else do you see in her March figures?

isolde.direction: The library, her thesis ledgers open: she has shown {player}, through one real household, how to read who is carrying whom, in a seminar voice with innuendo she never acknowledges, and corrected one of his words. She is showing him because he listens, which is rarer than she would like.

isolde.invitation: I am at Spell & Sip with a corner table and a small dataset I put together this week. Come sit with me for half an hour; the numbers concern you.

lines: *Two porcelain cups sit between you at the corner table, steaming steadily even though the waitress set them down ten minutes ago, and Isolde has her leather folio open in front of her shirtsleeves and charcoal waistcoat.*
I have been observing the households around campus that include a True Sire, {player}, and I took the trouble of calculating what you cost the women you spend time with.
*She turns the tablet toward you; the spreadsheet tracks hours, coffee, dinner crowns, and library study blocks across three neatly labeled tabs.*
In Case A, a third-year in Alchemy loses six hours of lab prep a week to your company, which is a steep outlay, though by all accounts your output when you are together more than covers her overhead.
*She reaches for her cup, her fingers steady, the surface of the tea still hot enough to fog the rim.*
Still, when I entered my own hours into the projection, I found I simply wanted you across the table from me.
That is to say, I am interested in testing your capacity for sustained returns under my direct supervision.
*She does not blink, setting the cup back in its saucer without a sound.*
I have left the Friday column blank on my sheet, {player}, so tell me how much of a deficit you intend to put me in this week.

isolde.direction: Spell & Sip, two cups that stay hot. She has presented, as a seminar, what he costs the women he sees and what he returns, and let slip one thing that was not innuendo before dressing it as one: she simply wanted him across the table. The Friday column is blank.

isolde.invitation: Come to my room on Lantern Row when you are free. I have a model on my screens that refuses to reconcile, and it requires your input.

lines: *Her room on Lantern Row is quiet, the wall of modern art behind the posh bed half in shadow while the two wide screens on her desk cast a pale light over her face.*
Look at the second screen, {player}—not a four-adult household, not five, just a two-party ledger, yours and mine, built properly from the ground up.

*You lean over her shoulder and see a clean, rigorous budget of shared hours, living costs, and stipends, except for the far-right column, which is highlighted in red and trails off into blank cells.*
My figures do not misbehave like this; I can usually feel an error in a sheet before I have even scrolled to the bottom, and this column has been wrong since Tuesday.
*She pulls open the top drawer of her desk and sets a half-empty blister pack of campus dampers beside the keyboard.*
I stopped taking them four days ago, which introduces a liability with no ceiling and no reliable precedent in any of the twenty-two households in my thesis.
*When she looks up at you, the seminar composure is gone; her mouth is slightly parted, and you can see every bit of the nerve it took her to lay the foil pack on the wood.*
I have stopped looking for a case study to tell me what happens when a woman gives a True Sire everything she has in reserve.
The column is not going to balance, {player}, so tell me if you are prepared to carry it with me anyway.

isolde.direction: Her room, the two screens lit with a ledger for a household of two, one column red that will not balance. She has stopped her suppressant; there is no case study for it and she has stopped looking. For once her face shows what she thinks. She has asked whether he will carry the column with her.

lines: *The two screens on her wide desk are lit with a sprawling spreadsheet, the glow reaching across the tidy shelves toward the modern bed you have already shared with her.*
I built this model three weeks ago, {player}, the morning after the first time you stayed here, because I wanted to see what our arrangement actually cost in practice.
*She highlights a row near the top: food, laundry, late nights, and a neatly itemized line for the physical wear and tear of having you in her bed.*
It balanced cleanly enough on paper, provided I held one variable constant and pretended I was only interested in short-term satisfaction.
*She opens her leather folio and slides an untouched blister pack of dampers across the desk until it touches your knuckles.*
I left that variable out because it ruined the symmetry of the sheet, and then on Monday I stopped taking these, which means the model is now entirely dishonest.
*She looks up from the screen, and for once her face does not hide a thing—she is watching you with quiet, unguarded intensity.*
I know very well what happens when a True Sire makes regular deposits in an unprotected account, and I have no interest in hedging against it anymore.
Check my working if you like, {player}, and then tell me what we are going to do about the rest of the night.

ifIntimate.direction: Her room, the screens lit with the model she built the morning after the first time he stayed, one variable left out. She has shown him the variable, that she stopped her suppressant on Monday, and that the model is now dishonest; she has asked him to check her working and decide the rest of the night.

lines: *Her study-bedroom on Lantern Row is dark except for the twin monitors on her desk, both filled with a single spreadsheet labeled for a household of two.*
*One column down the center is highlighted in stark red, every formula at the bottom throwing an error she hasn't fixed.*
You are looking at my five-year projection, {player}. Not 'guessing'—projection; there is a methodology.
*Isolde turns in her chair, and for the first time since you have known her, her mouth isn't tucked into its neat seminar line; her eyes are wide and unguarded.*
The red column is you. No matter how I weight the variables, the cost of you leaving breaks the model.
I spent three weeks searching the literature for a longitudinal case study on a partnership like ours, just to see how it resolves.
*She reaches back and clicks the monitors off, leaving the two of you in the amber light from the street.*
There isn't one. I am entirely in love with you, I have no precedent for it, and I need you to tell me what we do now.

ifUnprotected.direction: Her room, the screens clicked off, the red column that will not balance. She has said it is him, that there is no precedent in the literature, and that she is entirely in love with him and needs to be told what they do now. Nothing about what her body is doing.

lira.invitation: The sky is leaking again and the pond is very loud. Come to the Physic Garden. I have put my stones in order of how round they are.

lines: *You find Lira sitting on the mossy bank of the Physic Garden pond in the pouring rain, translucent blue, with a neat line of wet pebbles arranged beside her hip.*
You are here, {player}. Look at the third stone from the left. It has a white stripe all the way around like a belt.
*She reaches out a cool, slightly gelatinous finger to touch the back of your wet hand, then puts the finger in her mouth.*
You had the barley soup at lunch and also black tea with too much lemon. It comes right out of your skin when you get rained on.
*Raindrops hit her shoulders and sink right into her, making tiny concentric ripples inside her chest before she smooths herself back out.*
This is the seventh rain since I learned your name. Before that you were just the warm cedar smell by the greenhouse.
I do not usually count a person in rains. Usually they graduate before I get to four, and then they are gone.
Why did you come out in the wet when you cannot even absorb it?

lira.direction: The Physic Garden pond in the rain, her best stones laid out in order. She tasted the rain off {player} and named his lunch; she has counted him in rains, which she does with nobody, and asked why he came out in the wet when he cannot absorb it. Bright, literal, two hundred summers old.

lira.invitation: Come to my alcove in the Bathhouse. The water is very clean because I cleaned it. I want to show you my other shapes.

lines: *Turquoise light ripples across the dripping stone walls of her alcove, where Lira sits in the shallow hollow worn into the tiles below her neat rows of river stones.*
Sit down, {player}. You are making my knees nervous, and I just put them in the right place.
*With a soft liquid slurp, her curves fold inward into a stooped, heavy-jowled old crone, then flatten entirely into a three-foot-wide blue sphere with two polite eyes on top.*
The first one was the Dean from eighty summers ago, and this one is just a puddle that is paying attention. Nobody talks to a puddle, though, even if you are very bees-knees about it.
*She rises and pours herself back into the shape of a grown woman, her blue surface wobbling once before settling.*
I have never asked anyone this, and nobody has ever asked me. Which shape would you like me to be when we are being sweethearts?
*She presses both hands to her translucent stomach, which has turned a slightly deeper, warmer shade of violet-blue.*
Also, I am mostly stomach today, and it is three degrees warmer than the pool. What do you want to do about that?

lira.direction: Her alcove off the bathhouse pool. She took two other shapes to show him she chose this one because people talk to it, and asked which he would like her to be: nobody has asked her and she has never asked anyone. She is mostly stomach today, three degrees warmer than the pool.

lira.invitation: The pond is quiet and the frogs have gone to sleep. Come to the Physic Garden, {player}. I have a piece of news about my body.

lines: *The Physic Garden pond glows a soft, clear blue from the bottom up. Lira rises until her shoulders break the water, water lilies sliding off her head.*
Hello, {player}. I am mostly surface tonight, because the frogs were being very loud down at the bottom.
I stayed after the first-year Bloomology lecture on Tuesday. It was my hundred-and-fortieth autumn hearing it, so I thought it was time to raise my hand.
I asked the professor what happens if a slime takes a True Sire. Nobody had ever said, in two hundred summers, and I had never asked.
*She rests her chin on her translucent forearms at the stone rim, looking up at you with bright, round eyes.*
She told me I would carry a baby with bones, for three seasons, just like the girls with knees and elbows. I had always assumed that part of the lecture was not for me.
I found this extremely interesting. Then I thought about it for two rains, and I decided the father should be you, {player}.
You are very nice to hold onto, and your voice makes good ripples. Is right now a convenient time for us to begin, or do you have to study for an exam?

lira.direction: The pond at night. She asked the professor after her hundred-and-fortieth Bloomology lecture what happens if a slime takes a True Sire, since nobody in two hundred summers had said: she would carry a child with bones for three seasons like any woman, which she had assumed was not for her and finds extremely interesting. She has decided the father should be {player}, as plain news, and asked whether now is convenient.

lines: *A pale blue glow moves under the dark water of the Physic Garden pond. Lira bobs up beside the stone bench and puts two cool, damp hands over yours.*
There you are, {player}. I have been mostly wanting for four days now, which makes it very hard to stay in a bucket.
I finally raised my hand after the first-year Bloomology lecture this week. I had heard it a hundred and forty times, so I felt we were well acquainted.
*She pulls herself up to sit on the rim beside you, her blue shape rounding out warmly where her hip presses against your thigh.*
I asked the professor what happens when a slime and a human man go steady the way we do. Nobody had ever told me in two hundred summers.
She said I can carry a child just like any woman in the hall. Nine months, and a real baby with bones inside me, because of you.
I did not know I could do that, and I have never taken the tea against the Bloom. I think having your bones inside me for three seasons sounds very neat.
I have decided I would like that very much. Is that a thing you would like us to do too, {player}?

ifIntimate.direction: The pond at night. She has been mostly wanting for four days, and asked the professor this week what happens when a slime and a human man go steady: a child with bones, nine months, like any woman in the hall, which she had not known was possible for her and has decided she would like very much. She has asked, sincerely, whether he would like that too.

lines: *The Physic Garden pond is quiet in the dark, the water around the lilies glowing a soft, steady blue where Lira rests just below the surface.*
*She rises until her face and shoulders clear the water, droplets sliding back into her translucent skin without a splash.*
My core has been three degrees warmer since you came through the gate, {player}. It does that every time now.
I have known you for forty-seven rains. I never count rains for anyone, because people go away so fast.
*She drifts closer to the stone rim and rests her cool, bright chin on the back of your hand.*
You are my main squeeze—no, my steady. I have decided you are my one person for all the rains you have.
I have been in this pond two hundred summers and I have never told anyone that before.
When two people are each other's one person, {player}, what do they do next?

ifUnprotected.direction: The pond at night, her core three degrees warmer since he came through the gate. She has counted him in rains, which she does with nobody, and decided he is her one person for all the rains he has, never said to anyone. She has asked what two people do next. Nothing about what her body is doing.

lola-hopworth.invitation: Kitchen's cleared out and the pass is clean. Get down to the Honeyed Bee, love, I've got a knife with your name on it.

lines: *The pass at the Honeyed Bee is wiped to a dull shine, and Lola in her white chef's jacket shoves a scarred wooden stool toward you beside the big copper stockpot.*
Up you go, dear. Take the paring knife, take the onion, and don't butcher it.
*As you slice, she rests her palm flat over a linen-draped bowl on the worktable; beneath the cloth, the proving dough visibly swells an inch higher against her fingers.*
Tch. Knuckles in, {player}, unless you fancy flavoring the stock with your thumb. Do all the women on campus treat you like spun sugar, or does anyone actually make you work?
*She takes the halved onion from you, taps the blade flat against the board, and eyes you sideways.*
That stool came out of my mother's brewery kitchen in Butterford. Seven girls she raised round the copper, and I stood on that exact rung until I was tall enough to reach the ladle.
Haven't put anyone on it since I packed it up and brought it here.
So don't waste the perch, love—tell me what you actually do when nobody's fussing over your bloodline.

lola-hopworth.direction: The Honeyed Bee kitchen after service: {player} on the stool from her mother's brewery kitchen, where she stood as a girl and has put nobody since, a knife and an onion in his hands, dough rising under her palm. Blunt personal questions; she wants to know what he does when nobody fusses over his bloodline.

lola-hopworth.invitation: Come up the back stairs to the apartment. Put the kettle on if you beat me to the landing, I've got something on the table for you.

lines: *Her narrow apartment is warm from the ovens below, smelling of yeast and toasted grain, with Lantern Row glowing outside the window and Lola waiting in her pink sweater and white shorts.*
*She nudges a battered, gravy-spotted notebook across the scrubbed table toward you, then immediately turns to the counter of fermenting jars.*
Don't mind the handwriting, it's three years of scratchings and the plum vinegar in the corner jar is two hours off turning if I don't catch it—go on, open it anywhere.
*You turn a page: between weights for malted loaves and hop-shoot broth, it's a tight, vivid account of her mother's kitchen and seven sisters elbowing for the warm crust.*
The dampers on the bottom oven need drawing before midnight, and I told the cellar boy if he leaves the bungs loose again I'll have his ears—
*She catches you reading the margin notes, clicks her tongue, and goes quiet with both hands braced against the edge of the counter.*
Nobody's seen that, {player}. Not a soul.
I am not a sentimental woman, love, sentiment ruins a reduction faster than salt, and that bloody book is a great fat problem for my position on the matter.
Go on, then, say what you think before I snatch it back and shove it in the flour bin.

lola-hopworth.direction: Her apartment above the kitchen: the cookbook, three years of her mother's kitchen, shown to nobody, is open in front of him. She talked fast about ferments while he read, then stopped. She is not sentimental and the book is a problem for that position. She has told him to say what he thinks before she takes it back.

lola-hopworth.invitation: Down in the kitchen before the bakers get in. Come down while the bricks are still coming up to heat, dear, I want a word.

lines: *The Honeyed Bee kitchen is dark except for the orange glow through the oven grates, the air dry and fierce as the bricks come up to baking heat.*
*Lola stands at the floured wooden table with her palms flat on the boards, watching you come through the swing door.*
Good. Before the bakers come clattering in and ruin my head—listen a minute, love.
I've never taken a drop of damper against the Bloom in my life. Never saw the sense in souring good yeast when my whole purpose is to bear children.
Seven girls my mother had, and I always meant to fill a table of my own when the time came, only I never cared much who the father was so long as he wasn't an idiot.
*She steps around the table, stopping close enough that the flour on her knuckles brushes your wrist.*
Now I care. I want it by you, {player}.
Two parts plain fact, one part wanting, no garnish on the plate—that's the whole recipe.
So tell me straight, dear: are we putting this in the oven or aren't we?

lola-hopworth.direction: The kitchen at dawn before the bakers, the ovens coming up to heat. She has never taken anything against the Bloom and always meant to bear, and has never until now wanted it by anyone in particular; she wants it by him, said like a recipe with no garnish. She has asked whether this is going in the oven.

lines: *The Honeyed Bee kitchen is dark except for the orange glow through the oven grates, the bricks ticking as they come up to dawn heat.*
*Lola leans back against the floured wooden table, arms crossed, watching you come through the swing door.*
Come here, love, before the bakers turn up. We need a word with our clothes on for once.
We've been going at it like rabbits since we started, and God knows I'm not complaining—you're a proper feast and I've got the appetite for it.
*She uncrosses her arms and hooks a thumb toward the warm brick ovens behind her.*
You know I don't take dampers against the Bloom, and you know I've always meant to have a houseful of kids when the dough rose right.
What I haven't said is the other thing: it isn't just any child I'm after anymore. I want yours, {player}, specifically yours.
No garnish, no fuss—just tell me straight, dear, whether that changes the recipe for you.

ifIntimate.direction: The kitchen at dawn. They have been at it like rabbits, as she says; the other thing, never said, is that she wants his child in particular. She has asked, straight, whether that changes the recipe for him.

lines: *The Honeyed Bee kitchen is quiet before the bakers arrive, the big stone ovens ticking as they come up to heat and a dusting of flour white across Lola's knuckles.*
*She sets her palms flat on the butcher block, clicks her tongue once, and looks at you without picking up a knife.*
Listen to me, love, because I'm going to give this to you like a base stock—two ingredients, straight heat, no bloody garnish.
I have run at a rolling boil since I was fourteen, dear, and if someone couldn't keep pace I left them on the pass to go cold.
*She steps around the table and presses the back of her floury wrist against your cheek, her breath coming a little quick.*
I would turn the flame down for you, {player}. I would scrap the whole damn menu and sit still at the table if you asked me to.
I have never said that to a living soul, and my heart's going like a whisk in a copper bowl, so don't just stand there.
Tell me what you want from me, love.

ifUnprotected.direction: The kitchen at dawn, flour on her knuckles. Given like a base stock, two ingredients and no garnish: she has run at a rolling boil since fourteen and left anyone who could not keep pace, and she would turn the flame down for him, never said to a living soul. She has asked what he wants from her. Nothing about what her body is doing.

maren.invitation: Come to Boba Blossom! I got roped into sitting with the new exchange students and none of them have a single language in common. Save me, or at least come watch me show off a little.

lines: *You find Maren wedged into a corner booth at Boba Blossom, her fox ears swiveling between three bewildered freshmen.*
*She fires off a rapid sentence in liquid Veyran, pivots to high-pitched Kaelish without drawing breath, then rattles off four brown-sugar milk tea orders to the cashier in Imperial.*
*With a flick of her finger, a drop of spilled syrup lifts cleanly off the table's paper napkin and vanishes.*
There! Everyone gets pearls, nobody gets poisoned by a peanut allergy, and I only mangled one subjunctive.
*Her tail swishes, the ribbon at its base brushing the vinyl bench as she scoots over to make room for you.*
You're staring, {player}. People always think a girl in lace only knows how to order cake, honto ni.
*She leans her chin on her laced hands, eyes bright and sideways on yours.*
Vaelis-kor. No, don't make that face, I'm not translating that one for you—now tell me what you're drinking before my throat dries up!

maren.direction: Boba Blossom, a booth of exchange students with no language in common: she interpreted for all of them at once, delighted, and then called {player} "vaelis-kor" and for once did not translate. Bright, quick, pleased with herself; the word is a tease and a test.

maren.invitation: The girls just left and there are still three lemon tartlets on the stand. Come up to my room? I finished making something for you and I refuse to wait until tomorrow to see if it fits.

lines: *Her room smells of bergamot and warm ironed cotton, the tiered cake stand half-plundered beside her floral teapot.*
*Maren stands you before the heart-shaped vanity mirror, the glowing crystals ringing your reflections in soft pink light as she loops a black-and-pink ribbon cravat under your collar.*
Hold still, {player}, or I'll make the silk tie itself and it pulls terribly tight when it's showing off.
The third-years in my circle asked if I'm honey-trapping a True Sire for the Veyran Quiet Office. As if! My mother would die of embarrassment if my espionage looked this cute.
*She smooths the black lace points over your chest, her fox ears tipping back as she glances up through her lashes.*
Remember at Boba Blossom, when I called you vaelis-kor? It's High Veyran—it means 'the one I keep saving a chair for.'
*You blink at her in the mirror, and her cheeks puff out at once, her thumbs tugging the bow crooked.*
Mou, you're supposed to say something sweet back when a girl gives you vocabulary and bespoke haberdashery, aren't you?

maren.direction: Her pink room after her fashion circle has gone: she sewed him a ribbon cravat and fitted it at the heart-shaped mirror, joked about the Quiet Office, and told him "vaelis-kor" means the one she keeps saving a chair for. He took too long to react and she is pouting; she forgives within the minute.

maren.invitation: Come to my room when the halls are quiet. Leave the ribbon cravat on if you want, or don't. I have something to ask you without any tea on the table.

lines: *The glowing crystals around her heart-shaped mirror are dimmed to a low rose pulse, her tablet of flashcards dark beside an untouched teacup.*
*Maren kneels on the edge of her cushion-piled bed, turning her back to you so the thick plush of her tail rests near your hands, the black silk bow neat at its base.*
Nobody has ever taken that off me, {player}. Not back home in Veyra, not here—I always just flick my fingers and let the magic knot it before anyone gets close.
*She looks back over her shoulder, fox ears flat and honest, no pouting in her mouth at all.*
Untie it for me? With your hands.
*When the silk pulls free and falls across your palm, she shivers once and turns to face you, kneeling close.*
I always treated the Bloom like rain—you put on your petticoats, you take your damper with your morning tea, and you stay dry. I stopped taking them four days ago.
Kimi dake, {player}. Vaelis-na-kor—and don't you dare ask me to translate either of those right now, just tell me if you're staying.

maren.direction: Her room, late: she asked him to untie the bow at the base of her tail with his hands, which nobody has done, and he has. She treated the Bloom like weather and dressed for it; she has stopped her suppressant because she has stopped wanting to be dressed for this. She said it in two languages and translated neither, and asked if he is staying.

lines: *The crystals around her heart-shaped mirror glow a low rose, and the black silk bow at the base of her tail is already half-loosened, waiting for your fingers.*
*Maren sits back against her pile of frilled cushions, watching as you draw the ribbon the rest of the way off her.*
Don't put it on the vanity this time, {player}. Fold it up and put it in your pocket.
*She reaches out to curl her fingers over yours around the silk, her fox ears tipped forward, entirely serious.*
You've untied me before, so you know how quiet I get when the frills come off. I'm not dressing for the weather anymore.
I left my dampers in the drawer all week. The whole blister pack is sitting under my flashcards, untouched.
In Veyran we call a ribbon in a man's pocket a soren-vael, and I am never translating that for you out loud.
*Her tail curls warm and bare around your wrist, drawing you down toward the bed.*
Put it in your pocket, {player}, and tell me you know what I'm asking.

ifIntimate.direction: Her room, the ribbon off her tail folded into his hand: he is to keep it, in his pocket. She has stopped her suppressant; a kept ribbon means something in Veyran she will not say aloud. She has asked him to tell her he knows what she is asking.

lines: *The crystals around her heart-shaped mirror are dimmed to a low pink glow, and her tail curls over her lap as she unties the silk bow from its base.*
You've pulled this loose enough times, {player}, so you might as well do something responsible with it.
*She folds the ribbon into a neat little square, presses it into your palm, and closes your fingers over it.*
Keep it. In Veyran, we call a ribbon given like this kizuna-himo, and no, I am not translating that for you.
*Her fox ears flatten for half a second, her lower lip pushing out in a fierce pout at the mirror before she sighs.*
Ugh, I hate leaving a footnote blank. It means a tether you don't untie, okay? It means I'm yours even when you're not in my room.
*Her tail tips up to brush your wrist, her ears perking back toward you.*
So don't lose it, {player}, or I'll sulk for a whole minute. Now say something nice before I take it back.

ifUnprotected.direction: Her room, the ribbon folded into his hand to keep. She said the Veyran word for it and refused to translate, then, hating a blank footnote, translated anyway: a tether you do not untie; she is his even when he is not in her room. She wants something nice said back. Nothing about what her body is doing.

morwenna.invitation: Come to the upstairs room at the Honeyed Bee, {player}. My table is crowded with tedious people, and I require an excuse to clear it.

lines: *Four undergrads sit around the corner table in the upstairs room, leaning toward Morwenna in her black velvet coat and lace.*
Clara, your thesis is common, and Beth, your pulse has been racing since the stairs creaked. You may all leave us now.
*Nobody argues. Four chairs scrape back at once, and within thirty seconds you have the table and the teapot to yourselves.*
You may sit, darling. They were beginning to bore me, and the air in here was thick with their dampened little appetites.
*She pours tea into a single cup, pushes it across the wood toward you, and folds her hands on the table.*
A True Sire does not climb two flights of tavern stairs by accident, {player}.
*She gives you a slow, deliberate blink, waiting in the quiet for you to fill the space.*
You have been watching me from the doorway for five minutes, which means you came here to ask for something. Tell me what it is you want.

morwenna.direction: The Honeyed Bee's upstairs room, her court dismissed line by line and {player} kept. She has refused to ask what he wants and told him, by observation, that he came to ask for something; he is to say it. Low, measured, a slow blink; she enjoys making people say what they want.

morwenna.invitation: Come up to my apartment above the tavern. I have been reviewing my notes, and your name appears with an intolerable frequency.

lines: *The apartment smells of lavender and old paper, black candles burning in silver holders on the round table beside an open leather journal.*
*Morwenna stands by the black-laced window in her corset and tiered skirt, reading from a page covered in tight, upright ink.*
Listen to Tuesday: 'Subject three adjusted her collar four times in two minutes while {player} stood by the lectern. Even through her dampers, her heat was almost vulgar.'
*She turns the page with one finger, her voice dropping into a lower, measured cadence.*
And then the margin, written an hour later: 'I watched his hands on the chalk and lost twenty minutes of my own lecture. Exquisite, and entirely unacceptable.'
*She closes the book with a soft thud and looks at you over the candle flame.*
For three terms I have called this journal fieldwork. A pause for honesty, darling: I am withdrawing the word.
You know what it looks like when other women want you, {player}, because I just read it to you. Now tell me what you think it looks like when I do.
